newsitem.title: USA: Florida decision may free 1,500 violent inmates.
newsitem.headline: Florida decision may free 1,500 violent inmates.

text.p: The Florida Supreme Court ruled Thursday that the state could not retroactively force prisoners to serve 85 percent of their sentences, a ruling that could make some 1,500 inmates convicted of violent crimes immediately eligible for parole.

The court ruled unanimously that the state Department of Corrections could not expand a 1995 law requiring inmates to serve at least 85 percent of their sentences to prisoners who were already serving time when the rule went into effect.

Florida's attorney general held this year that corrections officials could use their discretion under a different statute to bar early release for certain classes of violent criminals, no matter when they began serving their sentences.

In April, the corrections department passed a rule prohibiting early release for inmates sentenced for murder, sex crimes, assault and a host of other violent offences. The rule affected about 20,000 inmates, some of whom began serving time nearly 20 years ago.

The new measures cut back on a rule that let prisoners "gain time," cutting their sentences in exchange for good behaviour while in prison. But the court said the department could not apply the rule retroactively without violating Florida's constitution.

"Given that the amendment applies to a certain class of inmates who committed their offences before the amendment's effective date, and acts to enhance the measure of punishment ... we are compelled to conclude that it violates the ex post facto prohibition," Justice Ben Overton wrote for the court.

The issue was brought to the court by lawyers for Richard Bing Gwong, who was sentenced to 22 years in 1989 for second degree murder and said he should be eligible for a chance to reduce his sentence under programmes in place at the time.

Department of Corrections spokeswoman Laura Levings said the agency was studying the opinion's impact on 20,000 inmates affected by the April rule change. She said approximately 1,500 of them might be eligible for immediate release.
The ruling came nine days after Donald McDougall, the prisoner whose imminent release inspired officials to toughen the "gain time" measure in April, was murdered in prison.

McDougall was sentenced to 34 years for the 1982 torture and murder of a five-year-old girl and was scheduled for release Dec. 31, 1992, but Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth revoked that gain-time release. McDougall was then rescheduled for release early next year and likely would have been freed in November had the court ruled sooner.
